Lariam Lament

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Could an unprecedented court battle reveal why 12 Irish soldiers killed themselves? The answer might just open Pandora's Box in South Africa.

Unique Selling Point:
Lariam is still widely prescribed in South Africa in spite of mounting evidence of its damaging side-effects. But, in a case not unlike the one which dealt a hammer blow to the cancer-causing pesticide, Round Up, the Irish government is being taken to court for ignoring those side-effects and knowingly endangering the lives of soldiers. In essence, this case, involving more than 350 soldiers, could have international repercussions including in South Africa.

Summary:
These 350 former soldiers all claim to have suffered damaging side-effects from Lariam. They were prescribed the drug while serving as peace-keepers in sub-Saharan Africa, and say their health hasn't been the same since. Their symptoms include mood swings, hallucinations, depression and what's known as "suicidal idealisation". 12 of their comrades, they say, killed themselves rather than deal with the debilitating mental damage wrought by the drug. One of the complainants in the case, Mark O'Sullivan, has built up a library of documents he believes points to Lariam as the reason for the suicides. The paper trail, he adds, implicates the Irish state in knowingly poisoning its soldiers: the drug continues to be prescribed by that country's military despite its manufacturer, Roche, having withdrawn it from the general Irish market in 2016.

To channel their outrage and help highlight their concerns around Lariam, they've formed a victims' support group, and have approached a lawyer to take the case to the Irish High Court. If they win, it'll be the biggest personal injury award in Ireland's history. More significantly, though, in the same way that the Round Up ruling is threatening Monsanto's financial prospects, a win for the alleged victims could open the legal floodgates against Roche as well a global medical fraternity apparently indifferent to the psychological welfare of its patients.

Press Release:


Lariam Lament
Lariam is a drug often used to prevent or treat malaria and is still widely prescribed in spite of mounting evidence of its damaging side-effects. For years, the Irish military has prescribed this drug to its soldiers when they're deployed to work in various parts of Africa. Now, hundreds of soldiers say they’ve suffered serious side effects including depression and suicidal thoughts and are taking on the government in unprecedented legal battles. Could the outcome open Pandora’s Box in other countries, including South Africa, where Lariam was prescribed.
Producer: John Webb
Presenter: John Webb


Script:


Lariam Script – Final.
VO: There are moments Tony Moore doesn’t recognise himself. Like the time he almost stabbed his wife.
ITV: Tony Moore: [01:28:40] I sat at this table, and we were just like me and your talking away and it was like someone put a black bag over me head that all I wanted to do was put a knife though me wife.
VO: Still married, it’s a dark compulsion he can’t explain.
ITV: Tony Moore [01:28:40] You know, why would I come up with a thought like that? It’s just, it's unbelievable to think about, it’s frightening.
Visuals of Tony Moore reflecting at the tram station into photos as a soldier.
VO: A soldier at heart, he joined the Irish military in 1983, and his country’s contribution to global peace-keeping took him to several countries in Africa. A decade later, he’s tram-driver in the Irish capital, Dublin. By his own admission, a shadow of the person he once was.
Moore walking out of shot from tram station.
VO: And that, he believes, is because of a tablet that was meant to keep him healthy.
SPC Document
VO: In 2013, the Irish subsidiary of healthcare company, Roche, updated the product information for one of its drugs. It included this section under the heading “Special Warnings and Precautions for Use”.
Section 4.4 in the SPC
VO: Among four paragraphs of bold print, this sentence stood out: “Cases of suicide, suicidal thoughts and self-endangering behaviour such as attempted suicide… have been reported.” If they develop, says the company, stop taking the drug immediately.
Table in section 4.8 in the SPC
VO: It goes on to say, in a list of “Undesirable Effects”, that the frequency of suicide and suicidal thoughts is “not known” but that other effects like anxiety and depression are “common”. (zoom into relevant sections)
The drug in question was the anti-malarial medication, Lariam – from the compound Mefloquine. It was discontinued in Ireland just three years later.
Moore Military pics
VO: But as Moore knows all too well, it’s been the Irish military’s anti-malarial drug of choice since 2001 – and still is.
ITV: Tony Moore [00:56:24] In 2005 when I went to Liberia, the drug was Lariam and Lariam only and the same with Chad. We had no choice but to take Lariam.
VO: After his six-month tour of duty in Liberia, Moore suffered from insomnia and muscle spasms. But, it was on returning from Chad, he says, and another course of Lariam, that the darkness set in.
ITV: Tony Moore [01:28:40] I had paranoia, suicide thoughts, I had depression. I had mood swings. I had anger and it was like being caught in this circle and couldn't get out.
ITV: Dr Remington Nevin [00:07:37] Some folks have told me it takes all of their effort to stop jumping off a building or to stop jumping into a fire or to stop putting a weapon to their head and shooting themselves. It's almost like something out of a horror movie.
LINK: (John on Skype) Dr Remington Nevin is an epidemiologist. He’s a former American army officer and a global authority on anti-malarial drugs who says that in the case of Mefloquine or Lariam, fighting malaria isn’t what it’s most effective at.
ITV: Dr Remington Nevin [00:09:59] when you look at drugs most associated with acts of violence, the top 10 drugs are all psychotropic drugs. Amphetamines, antidepressants and so on, with the exception of Mefloquine, which is an antimalarial. And so, I think that is further evidence that mefloquine really should be thought of as primarily a psychotropic drug with incidental antimalarial properties.
VO: Not that malaria prevention isn’t critical. In 2016 alone, it claimed more than 400 thousand lives – mostly in sub-Saharan Africa. Worryingly, some mosquitoes are showing signs of resistance to anti-malarial drugs.
Graphic of human brain
VO: Mefloquine crosses from the blood into the brain’s fatty tissue, predominantly acting on the areas responsible for fears and emotion.
Walking past the metal bench with footage of Moore transposed on the surface.
VO: And both those things have come to define Moore’s life.
ITV: Tony Moore [01:20:05] I came back from Chad, the psychological side effects kicked in and it was then I went to psychologists and I sat down and spoke with her and she says to me, it's the hallmarks of the side effects of Lariam.
City shots with file footage superimposed cutting to restaurant.
VO: Moore’s story echoed many others. So why, amid such controversy, would a country’s military insist on using Lariam? And, what, if anything, was the Irish government doing about it? It didn’t take much digging to reveal the answer to the second question.
CLIP: Paul Kehoe [09:26:33] Fundamentally, it is a medical matter that should be decided by qualified medical professionals and not politicians.
VO: In a debate in the country’s Parliament last year, junior minister for Defence, Paul Kehoe, made the case for Lariam.
CLIP: Paul Kehoe [09:31:40] The medical procedures involved in assessing personnel before deployment are designed to ensure that a person who may be vulnerable to depression or other mental health issues is not prescribed Lariam.
VO: Tony Moore was one of those people, but he was given Lariam anyway. (Medical File)
ITV: Tony Moore [01:31:32] I had anxiety and depression throughout in medical file. It was the army that put it there and yet they still went along and gave me the drug on two occasions. Yet they tell, they tell the world, we look after our troops great.
Dublin shots with file footage superimposed.
VO: Moore moved to the frontline of the battle for answers, becoming a vocal critic of the military’s policy, including on social media. (Facebook Action Lariam for Irish Soldiers)
Link: Moore’s activism didn’t go unnoticed. He says it made him enemies in the military establishment, but it also won him friends. One of those, a civilian who years before had returned from honeymoon a changed man.
ITV: Andrew Bryce [01:56:34]I felt shivery, I felt cold, I felt unsteady, I felt my balance was affected. What I wasn't able describe at that point in time was that I was actually suffering from anxiety, from depression, from other neuropsychiatric problems. I simply didn't have the language to identify them.
Andrew Bryce photos
VO: Andrew Bryce was given Lariam before honeymooning in Kenya in 1996. His wife suffered no side-effects, but his health quickly deteriorated.
ITV: Andrew Bryce [01:57:54] I was always travelling on business and working six to eight-hour weeks, no problem and suddenly I couldn't walk outside my front door (CUT to 01:58:41] for the first few years of marriage if I made it down the stairs during the day, my wife had to carry me back upstairs in the evening. That’s how bad I was.
VO: Unable to return to work, Bryce lends support to Moore and other soldiers in their quest for answers.
ITV: Andrew Bryce [02:07:09] The American army, the British Army, the French the Australians, a number of other major armies have all either banned Lariam or made it a drug of last resort. The Irish Army insist on using Lariam as drug of choice. It beggars belief. I cannot see any logic for it.
VO: And, says Bryce, ignorance of the side effects isn’t an explanation.
Andrew Bryce [02:11:31] I can’t understand how they could possibly not know. Like anybody who does any research whatsoever on Lariam knows that it's a dangerous drug. The FDA, the European Medicines agencies have both released safety, severe safety updates about the fact that Lariam causes permanent side effects and it may lead to suicide.
John researching in restaurant. List of suicides then graphic with the words “extremely unlikely” lifted from press report (http://www.thejournal.ie/shatter-link-lariam-suicide-defence-forces-956381-Jun2013)
VO: An investigation by the Irish national broadcaster – and verified independently – found that – between 2000 and 20012 - the suicide rate among Irish soldiers who’d taken Lariam was around three times higher than those who hadn’t.
VO: But, the Irish Department of Defence has consistently disputed this, saying in 2013 that an investigation had found it “extremely unlikely” that Lariam had played a part in the suicides of several soldiers. It also maintains that Lariam is the most effective drug for particular strains of malaria and, because it’s taken weekly, is ideal for military conditions.
VO: With little common ground between Lariam’s critics and the Irish military establishment, scores of soldiers, including Moore, are taking legal action against the State.
ITV: Norman Spicer [23:42:35] To date about 350 soldiers are in regular contact with my firm. My legal partners. At this moment we're currently gathering records and information and conducting meetings with this 350 but of that 350, we have instructions to issue proceedings on 100.
VO: The outcome could reverberate across the globe, including here in South Africa, because, fundamentally, at stake is the principle underlying all medicine: first, do no harm. And that, says lawyer, Norman Spicer, could shift the focus from the State to the doctors.
ITV: Norman Spicer [23:49:10] you cannot compromise your duty to your patient (CUT) So, I think you know the doctors in the medical core need to be aware of that, that they may possibly have to answer for any administrations of the drug that they gave out it's not, where it shouldn't have been done.
VO: But, as the wheels of justice slowly turn, the mental battle, says Moore, grinds on.
ITV: Tony Moore [01:18:54] You've everything kicking away inside your head and you don’t know how to separate and it just buzzes away and then the anger comes out and you either want to lock yourself away from everyone because they don’t understand what you’re going through
ITV: Remington Nevin [00:11:50] It's partly this disappointment, it's partly the sense among veterans that they've been let down by their leadership, that is contributing to the epidemic of suicide that we see. Veterans are so despondent at having been abandoned by their leaders that in many cases they simply feel there's no alternative but suicide.
VO: The Irish Department of Defence declined to be interviewed for this story because the matter is before the courts. Roche Ireland didn’t respond to our interview request. Here in South Africa, as elsewhere, Lariam is being phased out for commercial reasons.
ENDS.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Could an unprecedented court battle reveal why 12 Irish soldiers killed themselves? The answer might just open Pandora's Box in South Africa.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Lariam is still widely prescribed in South Africa in spite of mounting evidence of its damaging side-effects. But, in a case not unlike the one which dealt a hammer blow to the cancer-causing pesticide, Round Up, the Irish government is being taken to court for ignoring those side-effects and knowingly endangering the lives of soldiers. In essence, this case, involving more than 350 soldiers, could have international repercussions including in South Africa.
metadata.Summary: These 350 former soldiers all claim to have suffered damaging side-effects from Lariam. They were prescribed the drug while serving as peace-keepers in sub-Saharan Africa, and say their health hasn't been the same since. Their symptoms include mood swings, hallucinations, depression and what's known as "suicidal idealisation". 12 of their comrades, they say, killed themselves rather than deal with the debilitating mental damage wrought by the drug. One of the complainants in the case, Mark O'Sullivan, has built up a library of documents he believes points to Lariam as the reason for the suicides. The paper trail, he adds, implicates the Irish state in knowingly poisoning its soldiers: the drug continues to be prescribed by that country's military despite its manufacturer, Roche, having withdrawn it from the general Irish market in 2016. To channel their outrage and help highlight their concerns around Lariam, they've formed a victims' support group, and have approached a lawyer to take the case to the Irish High Court. If they win, it'll be the biggest personal injury award in Ireland's history. More significantly, though, in the same way that the Round Up ruling is threatening Monsanto's financial prospects, a win for the alleged victims could open the legal floodgates against Roche as well a global medical fraternity apparently indifferent to the psychological welfare of its patients.
